stem: Finding the kth smallest element without fully sorting is done by

options.text: Quickselect, which partitions and recurses into only the side containing k

explanation: Discarding the other partition gives average linear time rather than n log n. It is quicksort with one branch pruned, which is why the same pivot problems apply.

stem: Searching for the insertion point of a value not present in a sorted array returns

options.text: lo, the index where it would be inserted to keep the order

explanation: When the loop ends, lo has passed hi and sits exactly at the first element greater than the target. Returning lo rather than -1 is what turns a search into a lower-bound query.

stem: Merging two sorted arrays with two pointers is O(n + m) because

options.text: Each comparison consumes exactly one element, and every element is consumed once

explanation: Total work is bounded by the number of elements, not by their product. Concatenating and sorting instead would cost (n+m) log (n+m), throwing away the sortedness you were given.

stem: After the fast and slow pointers meet inside a cycle, the START of the cycle is found by

options.text: Moving one pointer to the head and advancing both one step at a time until they meet

explanation: The distances work out so the second meeting is exactly at the cycle entry. It is a result worth memorising, because deriving it under time pressure is not realistic.

stem: Supporting getMin on a stack in O(1) requires

options.text: An auxiliary stack of minima, pushed alongside each element

explanation: Each entry records the minimum at or below it, so the top always answers the query. Scanning would be linear, and a heap cannot respect the stack's ordering.

stem: Dynamic programming differs from a greedy approach in that it

options.text: Considers all relevant subproblem choices rather than committing to the locally best one

explanation: Greedy commits immediately and needs a proof that doing so is safe; DP keeps the alternatives and is therefore correct wherever optimal substructure holds, at greater cost.

stem: Relying on a hash map's iteration order in your logic is unsafe because

options.text: The order is unspecified and can change with capacity or implementation

explanation: Code that happens to work today can break on a resize or a library upgrade. If order matters, use an ordered map or sort the keys explicitly.

stem: Pre-sizing a growable buffer before a long append loop helps because

options.text: It avoids repeated reallocation and copying as the buffer grows

explanation: Appends are already amortised constant; pre-sizing removes the constant factor of the copies. It matters when the final size is known and the loop is long.

stem: Removing all elements equal to a value, in place, is done with

options.text: A write index that lags the read index

explanation: Read scans everything and write records only survivors; the gap between them is the count removed. It is the same shape as moving zeroes and as deduplicating a sorted array.

stem: Two loops, the outer over n and the inner over m, give
explanation: Writing it as O(n²) assumes the two bounds are the same, which is only true when they are. Naming the distinct sizes is what makes the analysis honest.

stem: A base class defining an algorithm's skeleton while subclasses fill in steps is
explanation: The structure is fixed in the base and the variation is delegated to overridden steps. Strategy achieves a similar end by composition rather than inheritance.

stem: Injecting an interface so the behaviour can be swapped at run time is
explanation: It moves the choice from compile time to run time and keeps each behaviour separately testable. Choosing it over inheritance is the usual application of 'favour composition'.

stem: The observer pattern is appropriate when

options.text: Several objects must react to a change in another without it knowing who they are
A class has too many methods

explanation: The subject depends only on an interface, so observers can be added without touching it. The cost is that the flow of control becomes harder to follow.

stem: A Java class implementing two interfaces with the same default method must

options.text: Override the method explicitly to resolve the conflict

explanation: The compiler refuses to guess, so the ambiguity becomes a compile error until you resolve it. Inside the override you can delegate with Interface.super.method().

stem: An overriding method in Java may return

options.text: A subtype of the original return type

explanation: Covariant returns let a subclass narrow the promise, which is safe because any caller expecting the supertype still receives something valid. Widening it would break that guarantee.

stem: An overriding method may declare

options.text: Only the same checked exceptions or narrower ones

explanation: Callers written against the base must not face new checked exceptions they never had to handle. Unchecked exceptions are unconstrained, which is part of why they are easier to abuse.

stem: The builder pattern addresses

options.text: Constructors with many optional parameters, where the argument list becomes unreadable

explanation: Named setters make each value's meaning obvious and let the object be validated once at build time. It is the standard answer to a telescoping constructor.

stem: Declaring a variable as List rather than ArrayList mainly buys

options.text: Freedom to change the implementation without touching the calling code

explanation: Programming to the interface localises the choice of implementation to one line. It is the everyday form of the dependency inversion principle.

stem: Overriding toString is worth doing because

options.text: Logs and debuggers become readable instead of showing a class name and hash

explanation: The default output identifies the class and identity but says nothing about the state. A good toString pays for itself the first time you read a log at 2am.

stem: Marking a C++ member function const promises that it

options.text: Does not modify the object's observable state

explanation: It also allows the function to be called on a const object, which is why const-correctness spreads through an API. Members marked mutable are the deliberate exception.

stem: Read Committed prevents dirty reads but still allows

options.text: Non-repeatable reads, because a row can change between two reads in one transaction

explanation: Each statement sees committed data as of when it started, so two reads in the same transaction can differ. Repeatable Read fixes that and still permits phantoms.

stem: A reporting table deliberately kept denormalised is acceptable when

options.text: The redundancy is documented and the refresh path is defined

explanation: What makes denormalisation a decision rather than a defect is knowing how the copies stay in step and who owns that. Undocumented redundancy is how data quietly diverges.

stem: Reading a query plan is the right first step when a query is slow because it

options.text: Shows whether indexes are used and where the row estimates go wrong

explanation: Guessing at indexes without the plan usually adds the wrong ones. Estimated versus actual row counts is the single most informative pair of numbers in it.

stem: The N+1 query problem is

options.text: One query to fetch a list, then one more per row, instead of a single join or batch

explanation: It is invisible in code that reads naturally through an ORM and devastating at scale. The fix is eager loading or an explicit join.

stem: Memory-mapping a file lets a process

options.text: Access its contents through ordinary memory reads, with paging handled by the kernel

explanation: It avoids explicit read calls and lets the page cache do the work, which is why it suits large read-mostly files. Write semantics and error handling become subtler in exchange.

stem: After fork(), the child's memory is usually

options.text: Shared copy-on-write, with pages duplicated only when written

explanation: Copying a large address space eagerly would make fork prohibitive, and most children immediately exec something else. The copy is deferred to the first write to each page.

stem: HTTP keep-alive improves performance by

options.text: Reusing one TCP connection for several requests, avoiding repeated handshakes

explanation: Each new connection costs a round trip for the TCP handshake and more for TLS. Reuse removes that per-request latency, which dominates on short responses.

stem: A CDN reduces latency chiefly by

options.text: Serving cached copies from a location near the user

explanation: Physical distance sets a floor on round-trip time that no protocol tuning can beat. Caching at the edge shortens the distance itself.

stem: git reflog is useful because it records

options.text: Where HEAD has pointed locally, so commits lost by a reset can be recovered

explanation: Commits orphaned by a reset or a bad rebase remain reachable through the reflog until garbage collection. It is the first thing to reach for after 'I have lost my work'.

stem: Caching dependencies in CI is worth doing but risks

options.text: A stale cache masking a broken dependency declaration

explanation: A build that only passes because the cache holds something the manifest no longer specifies will fail on a clean machine. Periodically building without the cache is the check.

stem: A Java varargs parameter is received by the method as
explanation: Because it is an array, it can be null when called with an explicit null, and it must be the last parameter. Both facts surprise people who think of it as a list.

stem: A static initialiser block in Java runs

options.text: Once, when the class is first loaded

explanation: Class loading is lazy, so the block may run later than you expect or not at all if the class is never used. Relying on it for side effects is fragile for that reason.

stem: try-with-resources closes the declared resources

options.text: Automatically at the end of the block, in reverse order of declaration

explanation: It replaces the nested finally blocks that everyone got wrong, and suppressed exceptions from close are attached to the primary one rather than hiding it.

stem: std::move does

options.text: Cast to an rvalue reference, allowing a move constructor to be selected

explanation: It performs no work itself; it only changes overload resolution. The moved-from object is left valid but unspecified, which is why reading it afterwards is a bug.

stem: Writing `for (auto x : v)` over a vector of large objects

options.text: Copies each element; `const auto &x` avoids the copy

explanation: Plain auto deduces a value type, so each iteration constructs a copy. For read-only traversal the const reference form is the default worth reaching for.

stem: Declaring a C function static gives it

options.text: Internal linkage, so it is visible only within its translation unit

explanation: On a function the keyword controls visibility, not lifetime. It is the C equivalent of marking something private to a file, and it lets the compiler inline more freely.

stem: An include guard in a C header prevents

options.text: The header's contents being expanded more than once in a translation unit

explanation: Double inclusion causes redefinition errors for types and inline functions. The pragma once directive does the same job with less boilerplate but is not standard.

stem: Undefined behaviour in C is dangerous chiefly because

options.text: The compiler may assume it never happens and optimise accordingly, producing surprising code

explanation: Optimisers reason from the assumption that UB is absent, so the effect can appear far from the offending line. That non-locality is what makes it worse than a plain bug.

stem: A switch on a String in Java compiles to

options.text: A hash-based dispatch followed by an equals check
A linear chain of equals calls only

explanation: Hashing narrows the candidates and equals confirms, which is why it outperforms a long if-else chain. The equals check is essential because hashes collide.

stem: In C, C++ and Java, the assignment operator associates

options.text: Right to left, so a = b = c assigns c to b and then to a

explanation: Right associativity is what makes chained assignment work. Chained comparison does not work the same way: a < b < c parses as (a < b) < c, comparing a boolean against c.
